entities.name: Maurice de Saxe
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Maurice de Saxe (1696–1750), the illegitimate but recognized son of Augustus II the Strong, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, emerged as one of the preeminent military commanders and strategic thinkers of the 18th century, profoundly influencing the art of warfare in Early Modern Europe. His career, spanning the service of both the Holy Roman Empire and, most notably, France, distinguished him through a blend of audacious battlefield tactics, deep understanding of logistics, and a progressive approach to military theory, solidifying his reputation as a master of maneuver and siegecraft during a period of intense dynastic conflict.

Saxe's military prowess became evident during the War of the Polish Succession (1733–1738) and reached its zenith in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748). As a Maréchal général des camps et armées du roi, he achieved decisive victories for France, most notably at the Battle of Fontenoy on May 11, 1745, where his innovative use of combined arms and defensive formations inflicted a major defeat upon the Anglo-Dutch-Hanoverian forces. Further triumphs at Rocoux (1746) and Lauffeld (1747), coupled with the capture of key fortresses like Maastricht (1748), cemented French dominance in the Low Countries and significantly shaped the terms of the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

His lasting legacy extends beyond his battlefield successes to his seminal treatise, 'Mes Rêveries sur l'Art de la Guerre' (My Reveries on the Art of War), published posthumously in 1757. This work, advocating for light infantry, combined arms, and a focus on maneuver over attrition, became a foundational text for military strategists across Europe, influencing figures like Frederick the Great and Napoleon Bonaparte. Saxe's emphasis on troop welfare, discipline, and constant training prefigured many modern military reforms, ensuring his theoretical contributions endured long after his campaigns.
